notes.meaning: God reminds Joshua that he is now an old man, likely around one hundred years old, and can no longer lead armies into battle. Yet large portions of the Promised Land have not yet been taken. God directs him to step back from active fighting and focus on dividing the territory among the tribes before he dies.

God lists the unconquered regions in the southwest along the Mediterranean coast. These lands include the home of the Geshurites and the five major Philistine city-states: Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. Even though the Philistines lived there, God treated this whole coastal area as promised land that belonged to Israel.

The list of remaining land moves north past the Phoenician city of Sidon and into the mountains of Lebanon. It covers the territory of the Gebalites, based around the ancient port city of Gebal, and stretches east to Mount Hermon. Strong Canaanite populations still occupied these coastal towns and mountain valleys.

God promises that He will personally drive out the Sidonians and the other northern hill peoples before Israel. Joshua must not wait for complete victory to take place, but must divide the land by lot in faith right away. This promise reminded the people that God would help them, provided they stepped out and obeyed His commands.

God commands Joshua to divide the land west of the Jordan among nine tribes and half of the tribe of Manasseh. Casting lots gave each group a distinct boundary and prevented future arguments over who owned what. It showed their trust that God would give them every acre He had pledged.

The writer explains why only nine and a half tribes received land west of the river. The tribes of Reuben and Gad, along with the other half of Manasseh, had already received their inheritance east of the Jordan from Moses. Joshua was to respect that earlier gift without changing their borders.

These verses trace the southern boundaries of the land conquered under Moses east of the Jordan. The territory began at the Arnon gorge near Moab and stretched across the high plateau from Medeba to Dibon. It covered all the cities once ruled by Sihon, the Amorite king in Heshbon, up to the Ammonite border.

Moses also conquered the northern territory of Gilead, Mount Hermon, and all of Bashan up to Salecah. This entire region had belonged to King Og, the last of the giant Rephaim people, who ruled from Ashtaroth and Edrei. God gave this fertile, elevated country into Israel's hands as their reward.

Israel failed to drive out the local people living in Geshur and Maacath in the northeast. Because of this failure, those groups continued living alongside Israel for generations to come. Leaving these ungodly nations in place later caused spiritual stumbling and political trouble for the nation.

The tribe of Levi was given no large district of land to farm like the other tribes. Instead, their livelihood came from the food offerings brought to God on the altar, along with special towns scattered through the other tribes. Having God as their special portion allowed the priests to focus completely on worship and serving the people.

Moses gave the southern part of the eastern lands to the families of Reuben. Their territory reached from the Arnon ravine in the south and covered the wide plateau around Medeba. Laying out exact borders ensured each clan had its own space and protected peaceful family life.

Reuben's portion included the city of Heshbon and several plateau towns like Dibon, Jahaz, Kedemoth, and Mephaath. Some places, like Bamoth-baal, had previously been used by the Canaanites to worship false gods on high hills. Later on, towns like Jahaz and Mephaath were set aside for the Levites to live in.

This list adds more cities given to Reuben, such as Kiriathaim, Sibmah, and Beth-peor near Mount Pisgah. Sibmah was famous for its rich vineyards, while Beth-peor was the site where Israel had previously fallen into pagan sin. These towns spread across the hills right down toward the northern shore of the Dead Sea.

Reuben inherited the kingdom of Sihon, including regions led by five Midianite rulers who had served as Sihon's governors until Moses killed them. The passage also notes that Israel executed Balaam, a pagan fortune-teller who had advised the Midianites on how to lead Israel into sin. God brought justice upon both the enemy leaders and the false prophet.

The western edge of Reuben's land was the Jordan River itself. This verse finishes the record of all the walled towns and rural settlements given to the clans of Reuben. It gave them a secure, recognized homeland east of the river.

Moses assigned the next region north of Reuben to the families of Gad. Their inheritance included the town of Jazer, half of Gilead, and border areas that had once belonged to Ammon. Israel did not take Ammon's lawful land, but captured territory that the Amorites had stolen from Ammon earlier.

Gad's territory stretched north from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh, running along the Jordan Valley all the way to the Sea of Galilee. It took in famous places from Israel's past like Succoth and Mahanaim, where Jacob had once met angels. This broad land provided green pastures and fortified cities for Gad's growing clans.

Moses gave another large region east of the Jordan to the half-tribe of Manasseh. Because this tribe was large and owned much livestock, half settled here while the other half crossed over into Canaan. This division fulfilled Jacob's blessing by giving Joseph's family a double portion of land.

Eastern Manasseh received the entire northern kingdom of Bashan, half of Gilead, and sixty towns captured by Jair. This rich territory was granted to the tough warrior clan of Machir, the son of Manasseh. Its wide fields and oak forests gave them plenty of grazing ground for their cattle.

This verse sums up the division of land that Moses handled on the plains of Moab before Israel crossed the Jordan. Recording the borders in writing created a permanent legal title for each family. It testified to how faithfully God kept His word to Israel before they even stepped into Canaan.

The chapter closes by reminding readers once more that Levi received no territory of its own. The Lord God Himself was their inheritance, just as He had promised Aaron and Moses. Serving God and knowing Him closely was a far greater honor than owning any piece of earthly ground.
